clue.text: A particle of cheese from Egypt packed between two cards

parts.note: second meaning: a soft curd cheese

indicators.note: something packed between two others sits inside them, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: queen and king, two court cards
the United Arab Republic, Egypt's official name from 1958 to 1971

explanation.surface: A crumb of Egyptian cheese sandwiched between two playing cards.
explanation.walkthrough: Two meanings plus a wordplay check: the Egyptian state's old initials sit inside the queen and king, giving QUARK.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a fundamental physics particle and a soft fresh European curd cheese.

clue.text: Chew, swallowing unusual snack — I'll swallow anything

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so these letters are rearranged
to swallow is to take something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a quid is a lump of tobacco for chewing
the five letters of the word, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone chewing gulps down an odd snack, boasting they will eat anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chew' looks like a verb but is a noun, a plug of chewing tobacco. The definition speaks as the thing itself, which swallows whatever falls in.
explanation.definitionFit: Quicksand engulfs any person or object that sinks into it, so it can claim to devour everything.

clue.text: Girl for instance upset gnome

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

explanation.surface: A girl, say, has knocked over a garden gnome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' looks like a garden ornament, but it also means a pithy saying, the source of 'gnomic'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome in its older sense is a short maxim or aphorism, just as an adage is a proverb.

clue.text: Central theme economist endlessly put in books

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
without an end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: John Maynard Keynes, the British economist
the Old Testament, a collection of books

explanation.surface: An economist's main idea, minus a tail, gets published in books.
explanation.walkthrough: KEYNE(S) loses its end, then the Old Testament goes inside it: KEYN-OT-E.
explanation.definitionFit: A keynote is the principal idea of a speech or policy, its central underlying theme.

clue.text: Astronomical feature discovered in Calcutta

parts.note: surface reading: something in space, a star or galaxy
setter's reading: the infamous Calcutta dungeon of 1756 bore the name of a collapsed star

explanation.surface: An astronomer in Calcutta has spotted something new in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Black Hole of Calcutta' was a tiny prison cell where British prisoners died in 1756; its name is also a space object.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a collapsed star whose gravity traps light and the notorious Calcutta prison cell.

clue.text: Press lord had to work hard

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the nickname of Lord Beaverbrook, Canadian-born owner of the Daily Express
second meaning: to toil busily, usually followed by 'away'

explanation.surface: A newspaper baron was forced to put in long hours.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Beaverbrook, the Daily Express proprietor, was widely known by this animal nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to toil industriously like the animal, and was also the familiar name for Lord Beaverbrook.

clue.text: A translation of bête noire

parts.note: a version is a rendering in another language

explanation.surface: Someone asks for an English rendering of the French phrase bête noire.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a request to translate, and the answer is in fact a fair English equivalent of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A bête noire is a person or thing one particularly loathes, which is also a sense of aversion, as in 'my pet aversion'.

clue.text: Clever card enclosing the present

indicators.note: to enclose is to surround, so one piece wraps round the other

explanation.surface: A witty greetings card with a gift tucked inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The present looks like a gift, but it is the present time: K(NOW)ING.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing describes someone shrewd, astute and well informed, a close synonym of clever.

clue.text: Obstreperous Gran is not under control

indicators.note: an obstreperous person is unruly, so these letters will not stay in order

explanation.surface: An unruly grandmother refuses to be controlled.
explanation.walkthrough: The unruly gran is turned into the phrase for someone completely controlled, the opposite of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone kept on a string is manipulated and dominated by another, like a puppet.

clue.text: Scoffed a portion of meat en croute

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is taken, so the letters sit inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the first two words

explanation.surface: Someone wolfed down a serving of meat baked in pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'En croute' means baked in a pastry crust; the answer runs across 'm-EAT EN'.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff food in British slang is to eat it greedily, so scoffed means devoured.

clue.text: Whatever happens, there are two sides here

definitions.meaning: second, cryptic meaning: every legal case or argument has two sides

explanation.surface: A fair-minded remark that every dispute has two sides, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a cryptic hint: in any case, legal or otherwise, there are two sides to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning anyway or regardless, used whatever the circumstances turn out to be.

clue.text: It produces illusory movement round the region

parts.note: the letter is round in shape
a part of the country is a region

explanation.surface: Something makes a region appear to move around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a preposition, but it gives the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is a 1960s abstract style using optical patterns that seem to shimmer or swirl.

clue.text: Refrain from betting everything — stay calm

definitions.meaning: first meaning, literal: not to wager even the clothes on your back
second meaning: the idiom for not losing your temper

explanation.surface: Advice to a gambler: hold back from staking it all, and keep cool.
explanation.walkthrough: To bet your shirt is to stake everything you own, so the idiom read literally fits the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to remain patient and not get angry; literally it describes declining to gamble away your clothing.

clue.text: A nasty trait — OK?

definitions.note: OK as a reply means settled; the question mark is surface

explanation.surface: Someone names an unpleasant trait and asks for agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying OK signals assent, the same as replying that something is settled and accepted.

clue.text: Eve had to make a fuss

definitions.note: a cryptic sense: what Eve did as Cain's mother
definitions.meaning: first, cryptic meaning: in Genesis Eve brought up her son Cain
second meaning: the idiom for kicking up a commotion

explanation.surface: Eve was forced to complain loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the idiom describes Eve rearing her first son.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to create an angry uproar; literally Eve, as Cain's mother, brought him up.

clue.text: Amazed, with mouth round, watching amorously as love disappears

definitions.note: boggling as a participle adjective, being amazed

indicators.note: turned round, so the letters run the other way
something that disappears is no longer there, so a letter is removed

parts.note: zero, a love score in tennis, the letter that goes

explanation.surface: Someone gapes, mouth open, while eyeing a lover as love fades.
explanation.walkthrough: Gob reversed gives BOG; OGLING loses its O (love) to give GLING.
explanation.definitionFit: When the mind boggles, a person is overwhelmed with astonishment, so boggling means amazed.

clue.text: King and prince upset team in race

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so it reads backwards

parts.note: eleven, the size of a cricket or football side

explanation.surface: A king and a prince knock over a team during a race.
explanation.walkthrough: GR is King George's royal cipher, seen on British postboxes; XI is a cricket or football side.
explanation.definitionFit: A Grand Prix is one of the major international motor-racing events in the Formula One season.

clue.text: Authoritarian rule gives man a kick

parts.note: a man's name, and a general word for a man

explanation.surface: A dictatorship gives someone a kick.
explanation.definitionFit: The heavy military boot became a symbol of oppressive, often military, domination of a population.

clue.text: Thousands back an agricultural worker

indicators.note: going back means the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a myriad is ten thousand, or countless numbers

explanation.surface: Thousands of people support a farm labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as support, but it turns the thousands round.
explanation.definitionFit: A dairyman works on a farm tending cows or handling milk, a specific kind of farmhand.

clue.text: Time man wanted desperately

explanation.surface: At a certain time a man longed for something badly.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long for something intensely, so yearned means craved or pined.

clue.text: Note private entrance to amusement arcade

parts.note: to log is to note down, record

indicators.note: the entrance is the way in, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A sign marks a private way into a games arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amusement arcade' is one phrase in the surface, but 'arcade' alone is the definition in its architectural sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A loggia is an open gallery with columns along one side, the architectural sense of arcade.

clue.text: Supervise the removal of trustee from 25

indicators.note: removing letters takes them out of the word that follows

parts.note: TR is a dictionary abbreviation for trustee

explanation.surface: Someone oversees getting a trustee off the board.
explanation.walkthrough: OVERSTEER minus a T and an R gives OVERSEE; the two letters are not side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee work is to watch over and direct it, the same as to supervise.

clue.text: Are all the competitors away from home?

parts.note: an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated a
the field is everyone taking part in a race

explanation.surface: A question whether everyone in the contest is playing an away game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' looks like the verb, but it is the metric unit of area.
explanation.definitionFit: Afield means far off, at a distance from one's usual base or house.

clue.text: Baby often choked — rehabilitated in a remote place

indicators.note: rehabilitated means restored into a new state, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An infant who kept choking recovers in an isolated spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes somewhere far from towns and civilisation, a very isolated location.

clue.text: Drink a litre in all

explanation.surface: Someone drinks a litre altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In all' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is the link and 'all' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Total means the whole amount or entire sum, everything counted together.

clue.text: Starts to operate properly, ensuring normal service

definitions.text: Starts to operate properly, ensuring normal service

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A shop or service begins working properly, giving customers normal service.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a business that opens, and the first letters of its last five words spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: When a shop or office opens, it begins operating and starts serving the public as usual.

clue.text: Mark two

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Mark ..., the American author
second meaning: an archaic word for two

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a verb or a stain; it is the author's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain is the old word for a pair, and the pen name of Samuel Clemens, whose first name was Mark.

clue.text: Turn more than intended, changing to reverse

indicators.note: changing means altering form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A driver swings round too far when shifting into reverse gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' suggests a reversal device, but it is simply part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A car oversteers when it turns more sharply than the driver's steering input asks for.

clue.text: With plenty of time to run, got landed in trouble

definitions.text: With plenty of time to run

indicators.note: something in trouble is disordered, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone with time on their hands got themselves into difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-dated bond or bill matures far in the future, so it has many years left before expiry.

clue.text: Queen's favourite part of the country

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Robert Devereux, Earl of ..., a favourite of Elizabeth I
second meaning: a county in south-east England

explanation.surface: The Queen's favourite bit of the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earl of Essex was Elizabeth I's courtier and favourite; Essex is also an English county north-east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names both Elizabeth I's famous courtier earl and a county in England's south-east.
